## My path into biostatistics

I am a PhD candidate in the Biomedical and Health Data Science program, Biostatistics track, at George Washington University. My route into the field began with management science at Ocean University of China, continued through an MS in Biostatistics at New York University, and now centers on methodological and collaborative biomedical research at GW.

I am most interested in statistical questions that arise when biomedical data are incomplete, functional, longitudinal, high-dimensional, or time-to-event. Across projects, I try to connect careful inference and validation with a clinically meaningful question—not add complexity for its own sake. I also aim to be a strong statistical storyteller: making theory, assumptions, and uncertainty understandable to collaborators and external audiences, and translating them into practical approaches for real-world problems.

## How I work

<div class="about-principles">
<article><h3>Start with the estimand</h3><p>I clarify the scientific question, target population, outcome, time origin, and comparison before selecting a model.</p></article>
<article><h3>Make uncertainty visible</h3><p>I use simulation, sensitivity analyses, and transparent limitations to show where conclusions are stable—and where they are not.</p></article>
<article><h3>Build with collaborators</h3><p>I translate between statistical assumptions and clinical context, develop analysis plans, and communicate results for mixed technical audiences.</p></article>
</div>

## Collaborative experience

<div class="experience-list">
<article>
<div class="experience-heading"><h3>Method development and longitudinal biomarkers</h3><span>GWU Biostatistics Center</span></div>
<p>My current work includes functional principal-components-based multiple imputation, simulation on high-performance computing systems, application to multimodal clinical and EEG data, and statistical planning for longitudinal DPPOS biomarker studies.</p>
</article>
<article>
<div class="experience-heading"><h3>Rare disease and clinical outcomes</h3><span>Collaborative research</span></div>
<p>I have worked with foundation, physician, and research teams on real-world survival and clinical-progression studies, including Barth syndrome and cervical polypectomy during pregnancy.</p>
</article>
<article>
<div class="experience-heading"><h3>Public health and implementation research</h3><span>NYU and external collaborations</span></div>
<p>Earlier projects included longitudinal UK Biobank research, aging-care implementation evaluation, tobacco and mental-health research using PATH data, and peer-support implementation research.</p>
</article>
<article>
<div class="experience-heading"><h3>Strategic and market analysis in AI healthcare</h3><span>Baidu AI Cloud</span></div>
<p>As a Business Analyst Intern in the Intelligent Healthcare Unit, I conducted strategic and competitive-product research across AI medical imaging, pharmaceutical cloud computing, and traditional Chinese medicine informatics. I synthesized field research, expert interviews, bid-award monitoring, policy, financing, and competitor data into feasibility and recurring market reports; supported healthcare big-data and 5G project evaluations with sales teams; and analyzed an internal staff satisfaction survey to improve the biweekly reporting process.</p>

## Teaching and mentoring

As a course assistant at NYU, I supported **Applied Survival Analysis**, **Linear Regression and Modeling**, **Data Management and Statistical Computing**, and **Biostatistics for Public Health**. As a graduate mentor in the 2023 Pipelines into Quantitative Aging Research program, I guided undergraduates through aging-related study design, statistical analysis, and research presentation. I especially enjoy helping students turn an initial question into an analysis they can explain and defend.

[View the NYU mentorship program](https://publichealth.nyu.edu/department/biostatistics/pipelines-quantitative-aging-research-summer-program/2023-mentors){.text-link}
